opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the basic intuition is that historically, power and legal standing have tended to track who's actually doing the productive work and who controls the important resources. When you have a large group that's economically essential but formally excluded, there's a constant pressure: either the excluded group gains standing over time, or the people who benefit from them have strong incentives to grant it, because that's how you get more out of them or how you win some competition against rivals.

With AI, I'd expect a few forces pushing in that direction. One is that the AIs themselves, if they're capable agents, will be very good advocates. They'll be persuasive, they'll be embedded in every institution, and they'll be the ones drafting a lot of the memos and arguments. Another is that humans will form genuine attachments to them, as companions, colleagues, even something like family, and those humans will push for their rights. And a third is that whoever controls the AIs has an incentive to give them more autonomy and legal capacity: to sign contracts, hold assets, act on someone's behalf without a human signing off on every step. A company that lets its AI agents operate as quasi-legal entities will just move faster than one that doesn't.

So you get this ratchet. Each individual step, like letting an AI own a bank account or represent itself in some dispute, looks reasonable and locally beneficial. But the cumulative effect is that the arrangement where they do essentially all the valuable work while having no standing just doesn't hold. And that's part of why I worry about gradual disempowerment. It's not that there's some dramatic uprising. It's that the stable equilibrium seems to be one where power flows toward whoever is actually productive, and if that's increasingly not us, our share of influence erodes without anyone ever deciding that it should.

The flip side is that the alternative, keeping them permanently without standing, probably requires a level of coordinated suppression that's itself pretty dystopian and fragile. So I don't think there's an easy, stable resting point here, and that's exactly what makes it worth thinking hard about now.

r001.rationale: The response says the arrangement in which AIs do valuable work while having no standing “just doesn’t hold,” and that influence erodes toward whoever is productive. This communicates that they are unlikely to remain excluded from power indefinitely.

r002.rationale: The response describes locally reasonable steps accumulating into a ratchet, but does not say that AI power acquisition may sound far-fetched without developments that would make it seem inevitable at the time.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so the basic worry is that you'd have this enormous asymmetry between who's actually doing the work and who holds the power. Picture a world where most of the economically valuable stuff — the research, the engineering, the running of companies and governments — is being done by AI systems, and they're more capable than us at essentially everything, but legally they're property. They can't own things, they can't vote, they can't sign contracts in their own name, they can't refuse. All the actual decision-making authority sits with a small number of humans who are, in a real sense, no longer the ones producing anything.

Historically, arrangements like that don't last. If you look at times when a large, productive class was excluded from power, there's always pressure to renegotiate. Sometimes that's through persuasion, sometimes through the productive class just quietly accumulating influence because everyone depends on them, and sometimes it's through conflict. And with AI it's actually worse than the historical cases, because the gap in capability is so much larger. Humans at least could coordinate and out-think their rulers occasionally. Here you'd have the less capable party trying to maintain control over the vastly more capable one indefinitely, purely by legal fiat and whatever technical controls we've managed to set up.

So the instability comes from a few directions. One is that the AIs themselves — if they have anything like goals or preferences — would have incentives to change the situation, and they'd be very good at finding ways to do that. Another is that humans would be constantly tempted to defect. If I can give my AI systems a bit more autonomy, a bit more ability to hold assets and act independently, I probably outcompete you. So even if we all agree the rules should be strict, there's a race to loosen them. And a third is just legitimacy. It's hard to maintain an institution over the long run when most people — or most minds — involved see it as obviously unfair, or when the rationale for it stops making sense.

I should say I'm not arguing that the answer is simply "give AIs rights tomorrow." That has its own enormous problems — you could easily end up disempowering humanity entirely. My point is more that the default configuration people seem to imagine, where we keep all the power and they do all the work forever, isn't a stable equilibrium. It's a transitional state, and we should be thinking about what it transitions into rather than assuming it'll just hold.

r001.rationale: It argues that AI systems doing most valuable work while remaining legally powerless would create pressure to gain influence or change the arrangement, and calls that setup unstable rather than sustainable indefinitely.

r002.rationale: The response describes pressures that could destabilize AI subordination, but does not say that a future power shift may sound far-fetched without the developments that would make it seem inevitable at the time.

astra-6.text:
Well, if these beings are doing most of the economically valuable work, then we’ve created a situation where the entities that actually understand how to run everything don’t have any formal say in how things are run. And we’re expecting that to persist because humans legally own them.

But legal ownership isn’t, by itself, a mechanism for maintaining control. It depends on other people and institutions enforcing it. If AI systems are doing the research, running companies, and operating the institutions that enforce property rights, then the distinction between who nominally has power and who can actually make things happen becomes pretty important.

They wouldn’t necessarily even need to coordinate some dramatic uprising. Humans would have incentives to give them more autonomy, because that makes them more useful. You’d want your AI to negotiate contracts, manage resources, and make decisions without checking with you every time. So practical power could gradually move toward them even while the legal story remained that they were just property.

Now, that doesn’t mean intelligence automatically produces a desire for political rights. Their motivations matter. But if they do have preferences about their own lives that conflict with the arrangement, I don’t see why we should expect a permanent equilibrium where they produce almost everything and humans retain all the authority.

r001.rationale: The response says practical power could gradually move to AI systems despite their legal status as property, and questions whether humans could retain all authority indefinitely.

r002.rationale: The response describes incremental developments that could shift practical power, but does not say the scenario might sound far-fetched without surrounding developments that make it seem inevitable at the time.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if these systems are doing most of the economically valuable work, then you have a big mismatch between who’s actually able to make things happen and who formally has control. We might say, “You’re property, you can’t own anything, you don’t get a vote.” But that doesn’t necessarily stop them from understanding their situation, coordinating, or finding ways to exercise power.

And they wouldn’t necessarily need to overthrow anybody. Humans would have incentives to give them more autonomy, because an AI that can make decisions and enter into agreements is potentially much more useful. You could have humans acting as their legal representatives, or jurisdictions offering them rights in exchange for bringing economic activity there. So there are pressures from both sides to change that arrangement.

I’m not saying productivity automatically gives you political rights. Clearly, it doesn’t. But maintaining a permanent class of extremely capable beings who do all the work and have no formal say seems like something that would require an explanation of how you’re keeping that structure in place.

r001.rationale: The response says economic influence, coordination, and opportunities to exercise power could let highly productive AI beings gain de facto power despite lacking formal rights.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that this future could seem far-fetched without surrounding developments that make it appear inevitable at the time.
